overview: This card covers the atlas’s approximate 1914-1938 Azerbaijan record, not all Azerbaijani history and not the separate modern azerbaijan-1994 card. Its first shape has a detached Nakhchivan polygon and covers 1914-1920; its second covers 1930-1938, joins the western area to the mainland and even contains the tested point for Yerevan. No feature covers 1920-1930 although the index continues through those years. The label spans Russian imperial collapse, a short independent republic, Red Army takeover, a Transcaucasian federation, rapid Soviet change and Stalinist terror. Neither 1914 nor 1938 is a true national beginning or ending, and the polygons cannot settle borders or control.

periods.title: Imperial war, oil and labor unrest
periods.summary: The atlas opens inside the Russian Empire. Wartime disruption struck an oil city whose multinational workforce had already built unions, negotiated a landmark labor contract and renewed mass strikes on the eve of revolution.

periods.title: Revolution, competing councils and civil war
periods.summary: Tsarist authority collapsed in 1917. Parties, soviets, militias and outside armies competed for Baku and its oil while class conflict and Armenian-Azerbaijani violence made political control lethal and unstable.

periods.title: Azerbaijan Democratic Republic
periods.summary: The National Council declared independence on 28 May 1918. A multi-party parliament met in Baku from December, but war, contested territory and dependence on changing foreign forces constrained the republic.

periods.title: Red Army takeover and a Soviet republic
periods.summary: Under military pressure, parliament conditionally transferred power on 27 April 1920. The Red Army entered and a Bolshevik-led Azerbaijan Soviet republic replaced the independent government.

periods.title: Transcaucasian federation and cultural experiment
periods.summary: Azerbaijan joined Armenia and Georgia in a Transcaucasian federation that entered the USSR. Literacy drives, new schools and a planned Latin-based alphabet transformed public culture while one-party rule narrowed political life.

periods.title: Industrial plans and forced collectivization
periods.summary: Oil-centered industrialization and worker housing accelerated, while collectivization, arrests and deportations tore through rural communities and pushed families toward Baku and other cities.

periods.title: Union republic during the Great Terror
periods.summary: The 1936 Soviet constitution ended the Transcaucasian federation and made Azerbaijan a separate union republic. Simultaneously, arrest quotas, secret police troikas and mass repression reached families, schools, professions and villages.

items.text: The 1914 feature is a two-part multipolygon with 165 vertices. Its main part contains the tested points for Baku, Ganja, Lankaran, Shaki, Quba, Shusha and Khankendi/Stepanakert; a detached western part contains Nakhchivan. Tested Yerevan, Tbilisi, Tabriz and Derbent fall outside. These tests only describe what the imported shape draws. They cannot prove who governed a village, where an army stood or which community lived there.

The 1930 feature behaves very differently. It is one 115-vertex polygon stretching much farther west, joining the Nakhchivan area to the mainland and swallowing the tested point for Yerevan, while still excluding Tbilisi, Tabriz and Derbent. The atlas also has no azerbaijan polygon at all from 1920 to 1930. A border that changes this strangely is a warning label: use it to find the region, never to settle a territorial argument.

Names need care too. “Azerbaijan” had long named a historical region in northwestern Iran. In 1918 leaders north of the Aras adopted it for their new republic, whose territory had usually been described through places such as Arran, Shirvan, Baku, Ganja, Karabakh and Nakhchivan. Scholars still debate the politics of that choice. This card means the northern state and Soviet republic; it does not quietly annex Iranian Azerbaijan into the story.

The separate modern card begins only in 1994, while this one stops in 1938. Those are database seams. Azerbaijan did not disappear in 1938, and modern independence did not begin in 1994. Keeping the IDs separate prevents the cleaner modern outline and present-day institutions from being projected backward into revolution, civil war and early Soviet rule.

sections.title: Oil city, revolution and a twenty-three-month republic

items.text: Baku entered the period as one of the world’s great oil centers. The boom had made fortunes for Azerbaijani, Armenian, Russian and foreign industrialists and drawn a multinational workforce into drilling, refining, shipping and rail work. Labor politics mattered: oil workers won what Ronald Suny describes as the first general labor contract in Russian history in 1904, then returned to major strikes just before World War I. Oil made Baku powerful, crowded, unequal and strategically irresistible.

After the 1917 revolutions, no single government smoothly inherited the region. Baku’s soviet, Bolsheviks, the Armenian Dashnak party, Muslim political organizations, oil employers and armed groups competed inside the city while Ottoman, British and Russian forces pursued it from outside. The Baku Commune held power from April to July 1918; a different coalition followed, then Ottoman forces took the city in September and British troops arrived after the armistice. “Who ruled?” could change within months.

Civilians paid terribly. Bolshevik and Armenian forces killed large numbers of Azerbaijani Muslims during the March 1918 fighting in Baku. After Ottoman and Azerbaijani forces captured the city in September, Armenian civilians were massacred. Donald Bloxham reports a very high estimate for the September killings but also stresses the complicated background and wider reciprocal violence; other scholarship disputes exact totals. The honest lesson is clear without scoreboard history: armed movements on several sides murdered civilians, and casualty numbers remain contested.

On 28 May 1918 the National Council proclaimed the Azerbaijan Democratic Republic. Its declaration chose a democratic republican government and promised civil rights regardless of nationality, religion, class, estate or sex, plus room for ethnic groups to develop independently. That sex-equality clause gave women political rights in law, a striking achievement for the period. A promise on paper did not erase war, displacement, class hierarchy or practical barriers to participation, so the card treats it as a constitutional commitment rather than instant equality.

The provisional parliament opened in Baku on 7 December 1918 in the former Taghiyev girls’ school. Its planned 120 seats allocated places to Muslims, Armenians, Russians, a German, a Jew, trade unions and business bodies; by late 1919, 96 members represented eleven factions. This was broader than a one-party chamber, although many members were co-opted through organizations rather than elected in a completed nationwide ballot. It met 145 times before its final sitting on 27 April 1920.

The republic also founded Baku State University. A September 1919 law planned faculties of history-philology, physics-mathematics, law and medicine, required Azerbaijani language study and admitted women and men on equal terms. Classes began on 15 November; the first year enrolled 877 students plus 217 auditors. Instruction initially relied heavily on Russian and recruited professors, which prompted debate, but the university survived every later regime change. Two Azerbaijani women were among its first physician graduates in 1922.

sections.title: Soviet power remade politics, borders and farms

items.text: Late on 27 April 1920, with the Red Army approaching, parliament voted to transfer power under written conditions: Azerbaijan’s sovereignty was supposedly to remain, the communist government would be temporary, officials and property would be protected, and fighting in Baku would be avoided. Those words are useful because they show what deputies feared and hoped to preserve. They were not a freely negotiated guarantee between equal powers; independent government ended as Soviet forces entered.

Soviet Azerbaijan did not keep one constitutional position. In 1922 it was joined with Soviet Armenia and Georgia in the Transcaucasian federation, which entered the new USSR. The 1936 Soviet constitution dissolved that federation and listed Azerbaijan as its own union republic. “Republic” therefore did not mean sovereign democracy: Communist Party power and decisions from Moscow constrained every phase, even while Azerbaijani-language institutions and local cadres expanded.

The early Soviet border was not drawn once by a ruler with a perfect map. Officials bargained over transport, pasture, population, security and administrative convenience, often leaving ambiguity. Later, collectivization made those lines painfully real. In 1930 the Azerbaijani secret police arrested and deported more than a thousand alleged kulaks with their families; officials then pressed others into collective farms. Across the Armenian-Azerbaijani borderland, more than 12,000 rural households were abandoned from 1930 to 1934 as people fled toward cities, neighboring republics or Turkey.

The Great Terror reached far beyond famous politicians. From 1936 through 1938, secret-police troikas processed cases without ordinary trials while numerical quotas encouraged executions, imprisonment and banishment. In Azerbaijan, targets included party officials, former non-Bolshevik activists, professionals, peasants and border residents. Wives could be exiled merely for being married to a condemned “enemy,” and children could be sent to orphanages and branded for their parents’ alleged crimes. Published totals vary, so this card does not turn one disputed estimate into a fact.

sections.title: Work, homes and an oil city under construction

items.text: Baku’s first Soviet planners inherited a dense center, oil works beside homes, poor worker housing and weak transport. From 1924 to 1927 they tested small houses, converted industrial buildings and denser apartment blocks at settlements such as Stepan Razin and Armenikend. Plans bundled housing with services, green space and shorter trips to work, and hundreds of units were built. Yet the need was much larger. A handsome plan did not guarantee every oil worker a sunny room, sewer connection or nearby clinic.

One visible innovation arrived in 1926: an electrified railway joined Baku’s oil districts to the center. The Presidential Library calls it the first electric railway line in the USSR. New worker settlements and constructivist clubs grew along the industrial landscape, while three successive general plans tried to organize the whole Absheron peninsula. Kid version: the oil fields got an electric commute before most families got anything resembling a modern bathroom.

Clean water was a major engineering achievement, but it arrived unevenly. Construction of the 187-kilometer Shollar-Baku pipeline began in 1911; water reached Baku in February 1917 at roughly one-third of planned flow. Extra wells, reservoirs and stronger pumps raised delivery to the stated design capacity in the 1930s. A city pipeline still does not tell us which flat had a tap, sewer or flush toilet. The sources support expanding supply, not a magical overnight conversion of every outhouse.

Sewage was part of the planning problem, not an already solved detail. The 1927 city plan called for unobstructed sewer and storm-water systems, and experimental blocks paid attention to ventilation and open space. Surviving evidence does not give a trustworthy republic-wide toilet percentage for 1914-1938. Urban apartments, older courtyard houses, oil settlements and villages had very different arrangements. When a source says “hygienic housing,” ask whether it describes a design drawing, a finished block or the home where most people actually lived.

sections.title: At home: relatives, rugs, iceboxes and no universal “normal”

items.text: In early twentieth-century villages, both small households of parents and children and larger joint households of parents, married sons, spouses and grandchildren existed. Work, property and childcare could be shared across generations. Collectivization transferred land and animals into collective ownership and helped break up many large-household arrangements in the 1930s. The evidence comes from censuses, archives and much later fieldwork, so it reveals patterns rather than one rule followed by every Azerbaijani, Armenian, Lezgin, Talysh, Tat, Jewish or Russian family.

Wedding preparations could fill a home with useful art. Museum collections preserve carpets, embroidered curtains, bedcovers, tablecloths, clothing cases, copper utensils and jewelry associated with late nineteenth- and early twentieth-century interiors and dowries. A bride’s handiwork could be both skill and household wealth. Region, class, religion and family choice changed the bundle, and Soviet campaigns later tried to remake marriage customs. So imagine many traditions in motion, not one costume party repeated identically from Baku to mountain villages.

Khadija Aghabeyli, born in Baku’s Old City in 1910, remembered waking to ice sellers. Wealthier homes bought blocks for wooden iceboxes; people with less money often bought small amounts of meat, fish or milk day by day. Her family prized freshly cooked piti, dolma, kebab and dushbara and considered yesterday’s food embarrassing for a guest. This is a vivid memory from one prosperous Muslim household, not a menu for the whole country. Still, “the ice vendor is coming” is a wonderfully pre-refrigerator morning sound.

Clothing and household goods also changed with place and income. The national history museum’s ethnographic fund preserves regional men’s and women’s garments, decorated copper vessels, felt, carpets, woven shopping bags and other everyday objects. Its own home is the lavish former mansion of oil magnate Haji Zeynalabdin Taghiyev, whose restored bedroom, dining room and boudoir show elite life. A museum visitor must not mistake those rooms for an oil worker’s lodging or a farmer’s house.

Literacy and schooling became a huge Soviet project. A republic-wide education commission began work in 1921; officials promoted free schooling, Azerbaijani-language administration and textbooks, and general compulsory education was adopted in 1928 and approved in 1929. Access still depended on teachers, buildings, language, gender and location. A decree could reach a village faster than a classroom, but the expansion created new paths for children whose parents had never attended school.

Written-language sample: `Yeni yol` (roughly “New Way”). That is the cataloged Azerbaijani title of a newspaper launched on 21 September 1922 by the New Turkic Alphabet Committee to promote a Latin-based script. It is a publication title, not a sentence overheard at breakfast. Readers were living through a real script transition: Arabic-derived and experimental Latin writing overlapped before the 1929 official switch, and a later Cyrillic change would again make family papers hard for grandchildren to read.

Medical training grew from a thin base. The 1919 university opened a medical faculty; a pharmacy technical school followed in 1925, Azerbaijan Medical University in 1930 and a pediatrics faculty in 1936 because child-health specialists were scarce. A specialized higher pharmacy institute opened at the atlas endpoint in 1938. These dates show institution building, not universal access. Rural patients might still face distance, few specialists and very different mixtures of household care, local healers, pharmacies and state medicine.

Children gradually gained dedicated services. A health-epidemiology department founded in 1924 monitored infectious disease; three sanatoria with 252 places operated in 1928; the medical university opened in 1930 and an independent pediatrics faculty in 1936. The same review says specialized healthcare had been extremely limited before 1917. The change was meaningful, yet a clinic in Baku did not mean a mountain child could see a pediatrician. Capacity, geography and political upheaval kept care unequal.

The new state museum was another classroom. Founded in 1920 and opened in 1921, it collected archaeology, coins, clothing, tools and household crafts; related museums and a manuscript fund grew during the 1920s and 1930s. Those collections helped scholars study the region’s past while Soviet institutions also decided which pasts to celebrate, secularize or condemn. Discovery here was not treasure hunting alone: cataloging a cooking vessel, textile or old document could preserve ordinary lives that political histories often miss.

ending.text: The 1938 endpoint is an atlas cutoff, not a collapse. The Azerbaijan Soviet Socialist Republic continued inside the USSR, endured World War II and later Soviet decades, and restored independence in 1991 while explicitly claiming legal succession from the 1918-1920 republic. The project’s separate modern card begins in 1994, so the missing years are a catalog gap rather than a historical void. People, families, languages, institutions and memories crossed every one of these political seams, even when governments changed the alphabet, economy and permitted version of the past.
